title: The Kalamas, alone
tomorrow: how can anyone love all beings like an only child?

cards: Three tabs open, three reviews, three opposite verdicts, and every one of them certain. A small town in old India had the same trouble, with teachers. The place is Kesaputta, home of a clan called the Kalamas.
Wandering teachers keep passing through. Each one praises his own teaching and tears down everyone else's.
Then the Buddha arrives, and the Kalamas walk out to meet him with the question they can't settle: some of these teachers must be lying. Which ones? Notice the opening that gives him.
A teacher, asked to judge his rivals. The easiest answer in the world is: me.

teach.b: He doesn't take it. In the sutta, his first words are that their doubt is fitting.

Then comes a list of things not to lean on by themselves: what's been handed down, tradition, rumor, a collection of texts, clever logic, how things look, a view you already like, a speaker who seems capable, and the thought, this monk is our teacher.
That last one includes him. Then the test. When you know for yourselves that something is unskillful, blamed by the wise, and leads to harm and suffering when you take it up, let it go.
When you know for yourselves that it's skillful, praised by the wise, and leads to welfare and happiness, take it up. And he doesn't hand them the answers. He asks.
Greed, hatred, delusion: when they rise up in a person, is it for welfare or for harm? Harm, the Kalamas say. They reach every answer themselves.
This is why Buddhists read the sutta as an invitation to test the path in their own lives instead of swallowing it whole. But listen to what it isn't.
It isn't believe whatever feels right.
The test has three legs: what it leads to, what the wise say, and what you've seen. And the town doesn't end in doubt. It ends with the Kalamas asking to be his followers.

how: In Buddhist study groups and retreats the Kalama Sutta is read and discussed as a guide to testing a teaching in practice, by what it leads to and what the wise say, rather than taking it on authority alone.

o: a town in doubt about teachers, told that doubt was fitting
a clan of monks who wrote down the Buddha's sayings
rival teachers who debated the Buddha in a town square

games.q: inside the town's question — tap the pairs.
p: a town in doubt about its teachers
on the list, so it includes him
lead to harm, the Kalamas answer
whose praise or blame is part of the test

s: the Kalama sutta says to believe whatever feels right to you
the test is what a thing leads to, harm or welfare, and whether the wise praise or blame it.
the Buddha's own authority is on the list of things not to lean on alone
"this monk is our teacher" is one of the things he names.
the sutta ends with the Kalamas still unsure what to do
they answer his questions themselves, and end by asking to be his followers.

games.q: your cousin's favorite wellness creator swears a supplement cured her anxiety, and thousands of comments agree. using the Kalamas' test, what's the first move?
o: watch what it actually does, and ask someone who'd know, like a doctor
trust it: that many comments can't all be wrong about something
reject it: anything a creator sells is false by definition
games.why: the sutta sets aside report and a speaker's charm, but it doesn't say reject everything: it asks what a thing leads to, and what the wise say about it.

practice: Write down one thing you believe mostly because everyone says it, on any scrap of paper.
Hold it, and give the sutta's three questions one slow breath each: does it lead to harm or welfare? would the wise praise it? what have I actually seen?
Then rest with the paper in your hand and let the answers come as slowly as they need to.

wordCard.voice: The Kalamas: the townspeople who told the Buddha they were in doubt about every teacher, and heard that their doubt was fitting.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the clan in the town of Kesaputta.

carryVoice: Here's the line: know for yourselves, by what a thing does, not on a whim. Sutta read, and a town left thinking.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65 (Kesaputtiya Sutta, to the Kalamas)
